outcome: The general bipartite-graph conjecture remains open as of 26 September 2026; the several post-2024 papers found (subdivisions/theta substitutions, hypergraph analogues, Cayley/conjugacy-class kernels, spectral and tournament variants) each settle only a restricted subclass or a different (related) statement, not the conjecture as stated, and DeepMind's AlphaEvolve system was explicitly tested against it in 2025-2026 and found no counterexample.

ai.basis_quote: For well-known open conjectures like Sidorenko's conjecture, AlphaEvolve generally was able to locate the previously known candidates for optimizers (that are conjectured to be optimal), but did not locate any stronger counterexamples: thus, we did not disprove any major open conjecture.

summary: Sidorenko's conjecture (that homomorphism densities of bipartite graphs H into any graph/graphon G are minimized by quasirandom G) remains open in general, per the live Wikipedia article and every source consulted. The post-January-2024 literature is active but consists entirely of case/variant results that do not touch the general statement: (1) arXiv:2408.03491 (Aug 2024, published in Combinatorics, Probability and Computing 2025) proves the Sidorenko property for graphs formed by theta-substitutions/subdivisions of a complete graph -- a genuine case-narrowing result (a subclass of bipartite graphs is settled) but not a change to the conjecture itself, and it discloses no AI involvement; (2) arXiv:2509.08680 addresses a hypergraph analogue (a related, differently-stated problem, per Wikipedia's own note that the hypergraph version is already known false in general); (3) arXiv:2606.15368 and arXiv:2606.23018 prove Sidorenko-type inequalities for Cayley/conjugacy-class kernels, a restricted algebraic setting; (4) arXiv:2605.26614 is a spectral variant; (5) arXiv:2512.11222 is a tournament analogue. None of these are cases obtained by pure restriction of the stated bipartite-graph/graphon conjecture in a way that would change what a careful reader would write in this bullet, except arguably (1), which I record as a genuine partial-style case result but which does not move the bullet's headline status since the conjecture as a whole is still open and this is one of many known partial classes (paths, trees, even cycles, K_{s,t}, hypercubes, etc., already known before 2024). The one directly AI-relevant fact found is that Google DeepMind's AlphaEvolve system (an LLM-driven evolutionary search agent) was run against Sidorenko's conjecture as one of 67 benchmark open problems in the paper 'Mathematical exploration and discovery at scale' (arXiv:2511.02864, Nov 2025; also written up on Terence Tao's blog, who is a co-author) and a companion public repository (google-deepmind/alphaevolve_repository_of_problems, problem #26/#11 depending on listing). The authors state plainly that AlphaEvolve located the already-known conjectured extremal graphs but did not find any counterexample -- a null result, not a resolution, bound-move, or withdrawn claim, so it does not change status or warrant 'progress'/'incident' coding, but it is a well-documented, authors'-own-account instance of a frontier AI system being pointed at exactly this conjecture and failing to move it. A separate, independent effort (Duke University's 'AI-powered Discovery of Counterexamples in Combinatorics' project report) also used reinforcement learning to search for Sidorenko counterexamples on graphs up to 15 vertices and likewise found none (searches converged to the complete graph). Both AI efforts are negative results consistent with the conjecture likely being true, or at least not falsifiable by search at these scales. I classify the record as open/no_change_found because no source changes what should be written in the Wikipedia bullet, while documenting the AI search efforts in ai_role/ai fields as the most relevant AI-adjacent fact even though ai_role is coded 'none' (no AI system produced or contributed to mathematics that appears in any accepted result on this problem -- it only searched and found nothing).
competing_reading: One could argue arXiv:2408.03491's theta-substitution/subdivision result is a 'case settled' under §3.1 (restricting the class of bipartite graphs H to a specific structural family and proving Sidorenko holds for it), which would justify status 'partial' with resolution_direction 'confirmed' rather than 'open'. I did not take this reading because subclass-widening results of exactly this kind (recursive constructions producing new Sidorenko graphs from old ones) have been a continuous feature of this literature since well before 2024 and were already true of the pre-2024 state of the article (paths, trees, even cycles, hypercubes, blow-ups, etc. were already known); treating every such incremental subclass paper as a status-changing 'partial' would make nearly every survey-style conjecture with an active literature default to 'partial' regardless of whether the frozen bullet's substance changed. A stricter reader applying §3.1 literally ('does this change what a careful person would write in this bullet's entry') might reasonably choose 'partial' here; I flag this as a genuine judgment call.
what_would_settle_it: A resolution (proof or explicit counterexample) for the full bipartite-graph/graphon statement, or a claim of one that a subsequent digestion could confirm or reject; short of that, a statement from Wikipedia editors or a survey author that a specific post-2024 subclass result is considered to have narrowed the open cases in a way the community treats as noteworthy (e.g. resolving the K5,5-minus-C10 'Möbius strip' case, which multiple sources confirm is still the smallest known open case as of the AlphaEvolve paper).
